control_ladder.note_beginner: Thyme likes dry soil, but a plant left bone dry through a heat wave is the one mites take over. In a long dry spell, give it a single deep soak and then let it dry out again, rather than a splash of water every day.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The lever is drought stress, not the moisture level itself: soak deeply during a prolonged dry stretch, then leave it alone until the ground has dried out. Frequent light watering would trade a mite flare for the root rot that actually kills thyme.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Blast the mites off with the hose on a hard setting, working in under the sprigs as well as over the top. Thyme's stems are woody enough to take it, and you will need to repeat while the hot, dry weather holds.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A thyme plant is a tough enough subshrub to hose forcefully, and repetition is what stops a colony rebuilding; the low, spreading habit means the water has to come in from the side to reach anything. Take the pass in the morning so the mat is dry by evening.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the speckling keeps spreading, reach for insecticidal soap, sold for exactly these soft-bodied pests. It kills only what the spray directly wets, so on leaves this small, work slowly and get in under the mat as well as over the top.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap leaves no residual, so it only kills what it lands on, and on a dense low mat that means getting the nozzle in under the canopy. Skip it during a heat wave: it burns foliage on a plant already hot and short of water, which is exactly when mite numbers peak.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Fine yellow stippling on the small leaves, sometimes with faint webbing, most likely during a stretch of hot, dry weather. Thyme carries about as light a pest load as any herb in the garden, so this is a weather-driven flare rather than a standing problem.
symptoms_seasoned.why: Dropped 'or on stressed or crowded plants': nothing read attributes mites on thyme to stress or crowding, and the one source that names crowding attaches it to APHIDS ('Aphids are common in rapidly growing, succulent plants that are in crowded conditions'), so the attribute looks transferred from the aphid entry. Also moved the webbing off 'the stems', which no source states.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: iastate_ext: 'Spider mites can occasionally become a problem during hot, dry weather.' + 'Thyme has relatively few serious pest and disease issues when planted in suitable conditions.' | ucanr_marin_mg: 'Thyme is fairly pest and disease resistant, although spider mites can be a problem in dry weather.' | ncsu_ext: 'This genus has no serious insect or disease problems.' | uf_ifas (Pasco, TEMPLATE-WEAK): 'Spider mites are tiny pests that feed on plant sap, causing stippling and webbing on leaves.'

symptoms_beginner.new: Tiny yellow speckles across the leaves, sometimes with a little fine webbing. It shows up in hot, dry weather and is usually minor, since thyme sees very few pests.
symptoms_beginner.why: Same webbing placement fix as the seasoned register: the record said 'webbing on the stems' and the only source that describes the webbing puts it on leaves. Correcting one register and leaving the other would have left the wrong placement live.
symptoms_beginner.anchor: uf_ifas (Pasco, TEMPLATE-WEAK): 'causing stippling and webbing on leaves.' | iastate_ext: 'Spider mites can occasionally become a problem during hot, dry weather.'

cause_seasoned.new: Tiny sap-feeding mites, closer kin to spiders than to insects, that flare in hot, dry weather. Thyme carries a light pest load and this is one of only a handful of pests any extension source reports on it.
cause_seasoned.why: Removed 'is typically grown with little or no pesticide': no anchor in any of the eleven documents read, none of which makes a statement about pesticide practice on thyme. Added the not-an-insect fact, which is the biology behind this pass flipping the pinned type from insect to mite.
cause_seasoned.anchor: umd_ext: 'Spider mites are tiny, eight-legged non-insects (related to spiders) about the size of a punctuation period.' | iastate_ext: 'Thyme has relatively few serious pest and disease issues when planted in suitable conditions.' + 'Spider mites can occasionally become a problem during hot, dry weather. Aphids are occasional pests.'

cause_beginner.new: Very small sap-sucking mites, more closely related to spiders than to insects. They build up during hot, dry weather, and thyme is a plant they bother only occasionally.
cause_beginner.why: Removed 'rarely needs spraying', the same unanchored pesticide-practice claim the seasoned register carried. Added the not-an-insect fact.
cause_beginner.anchor: umd_ext: 'Spider mites are tiny, eight-legged non-insects (related to spiders) about the size of a punctuation period.' | ncsu_ext: 'This genus has no serious insect or disease problems.'

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: Hose the mites off and keep repeating while the hot, dry weather lasts; step up to insecticidal soap only if numbers keep climbing. Water deeply through a long dry spell rather than letting the plant bake, but do not shift to frequent light watering.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: Removed 'A hard harvest or shear removes much of the infested growth at once': no source says shearing removes mites. ISU's shearing guidance is about habit and rejuvenating declining growth, a vigor claim, so the mite-control reading was a modeled inference. Replaced it with the drought guidance ISU actually publishes, which is also the ladder's first rung.
organic_treatment_seasoned.anchor: clemson_hgic (herb-general scope): 'can be discouraged by spraying the plants with a strong stream of water regularly during periods of drought' | iastate_ext: 'Water plants during prolonged dry periods, but avoid frequent irrigation.'

organic_treatment_beginner.new: Wash them off with the hose every few days while the hot weather lasts. Use insecticidal soap only if there are a lot. In a long dry spell, give the plant one deep watering rather than letting it bake.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: Removed 'Cutting the plant back also removes most of them', the beginner-register form of the same unanchored shearing claim.
organic_treatment_beginner.anchor: clemson_hgic (herb-general scope): 'spraying the plants with a strong stream of water regularly during periods of drought' | iastate_ext: 'Water plants during prolonged dry periods, but avoid frequent irrigation.'

prevention_seasoned.new: Give plants full sun and room around them, and keep a pot from baking dry through a heat wave. The flare follows hot, dry weather, so the summer watering habit is the part to get right.
prevention_seasoned.why: Removed 'Vigorous, unstressed thyme rarely attracts mites': no anchor. Nothing read links thyme's vigor to whether mites find it, and the sentence is the same vigor-repels-pests construction the aphid entry states outright backwards.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: iastate_ext: 'Good drainage, proper spacing, and periodic replacement of aging plants help minimize these issues.' + 'Water plants during prolonged dry periods, but avoid frequent irrigation.' | ucanr_marin_mg: 'Prune for good air circulation.' + 'spider mites can be a problem in dry weather'

prevention_beginner.new: Grow thyme in full sun with space around each plant, and keep pots from baking dry in a heat wave. Mites turn up in hot, dry spells, so that is when to watch for them.
prevention_beginner.why: Removed 'Healthy plants rarely get mites': no anchor, and it is the beginner form of the vigor-repels-pests claim.
prevention_beginner.anchor: iastate_ext: 'Water plants during prolonged dry periods, but avoid frequent irrigation.' + 'Spider mites can occasionally become a problem during hot, dry weather.'

control_ladder.note_beginner: Feed thyme sparingly, or not at all. Extra fertilizer and rich ground give it soft, sappy new shoots, which is exactly what aphids breed on, and thyme is happier on poor dry soil in any case.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Lean ground works by withholding the soft, succulent tissue aphid colonies need, not by making the plant tough enough to fight them off. Overfeeding buys weak, sprawling stems and weaker aromatic oils along with the aphids, so restraint costs nothing here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pinch off any sprig that stays covered and take it to the trash, not back onto the bed. On a plant this small, a few snips take out most of a colony.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing weak and infested growth is the standard herb-bed answer, and on thyme it doubles as the light shaping the plant wants after flowering. The clippings should leave the bed, not land at the base of the plant.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Thyme's low mat means the hose has to come in sideways: angle a firm spray up under the shoots and most of the colony goes with it, and few aphids climb back afterward.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Thyme's wiry stems take a forceful jet that would flatten a seedling, so this is a real first move rather than a token one. Repeat as new clusters appear, and go in the morning so the canopy dries.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a colony holds on after a couple of hosings, insecticidal soap will finish it. It kills only what the spray actually wets, so cover the shoots properly instead of misting the top of the plant.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: This is the last step the problem should ever need on thyme, where aphids are reported as occasional rather than damaging. Soap leaves nothing behind, so predators arriving later are unharmed, and a repeat pass catches what the first missed.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Occasional colonies of small soft-bodied insects on the stems and under the leaves, most likely where plants are crowded or have been pushed along with rich soil or fertilizer. Rarely a serious problem on thyme.
symptoms_seasoned.why: 'On tender new growth' is unsupported by anything read. Two documents give a feeding site and they do not agree in scope: umd_ext puts aphids 'on plant stems and on leaves', the uf_ifas Pasco post says undersides of leaves. My first draft took the narrower one, which rested the placement on the template post alone; it is widened here to what the non-template source actually says, with the template as the corroborating half rather than the load-bearing one. 'Stressed' is also unsupported, and the source that names crowding pairs it with rapid succulent growth, which the record dropped, keeping only the half that reads as a stress story.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: umd_ext: 'on plant stems and on leaves' | clemson_hgic (herb-general scope): 'Aphids and spider mites can be a problem. Aphids are common in rapidly growing, succulent plants that are in crowded conditions.' | uf_ifas (Pasco, TEMPLATE-WEAK): 'These small, soft-bodied insects can cluster on the undersides of leaves, sucking sap and causing wilting.' | iastate_ext: 'Aphids are occasional pests.'

symptoms_beginner.new: Small soft bugs clustered on the stems and under the leaves now and again, usually where plants are crowded or growing soft and sappy in rich soil. Rarely a big deal on thyme.
symptoms_beginner.why: Same two fixes as the seasoned register: the feeding site moves off 'tender new growth' and is stated at the width umd_ext gives it rather than narrowed onto the template post, and 'stressed' is replaced by the growth condition the source actually names.
symptoms_beginner.anchor: umd_ext: 'on plant stems and on leaves' | clemson_hgic (herb-general scope): 'Aphids are common in rapidly growing, succulent plants that are in crowded conditions.' | uf_ifas (Pasco, TEMPLATE-WEAK): 'can cluster on the undersides of leaves'

cause_seasoned.new: Sap-feeding insects that turn up on thyme now and then. They multiply on soft, fast growth, which is why a plant on lean, dry ground sees fewer of them than a well-fed one.
cause_seasoned.why: The record's cause field said only that thyme 'is fairly pest-resistant and seldom needs treatment', which is the same treatment-practice claim the reviewer found unanchored on the mite entry, and it left the entry with no mechanism at all. The published mechanism belongs here, stated the right way round.

cause_beginner.new: Small sap-sucking insects that show up now and then. They build up on soft, sappy growth, so thyme kept lean and dry gets fewer of them.
cause_beginner.why: Removed 'rarely needs spraying' (the unanchored treatment-practice claim) and put the sourced mechanism in its place, matching the seasoned register.
cause_beginner.anchor: clemson_hgic (herb-general scope): 'Aphids are common in rapidly growing, succulent plants.' | iastate_ext: 'Thyme grows best in full sun and well-drained soil. It tolerates poor, dry, and rocky sites where many other plants struggle.'

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: Hose the clusters off and pinch out any shoot that stays covered, then use insecticidal soap only if numbers keep building. Trimmings leave the bed; do not let them drop at the foot of the plant.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: Removed 'Improving airflow and removing stress usually resolves it': no source says airflow controls aphids, and no source attributes aphids on thyme to stress. The herb-general sentence that does exist supports sanitation and removal of infested growth, which is a different rung and is what the ladder now carries.
organic_treatment_seasoned.anchor: clemson_hgic (herb-general scope): 'The best defenses against pests on herbs are proper growing conditions, good sanitation, removal of weak or infested growth, and regular pruning.' | uf_ifas (Pasco, TEMPLATE-WEAK): 'Use a strong jet of water to dislodge aphids from the plant. Spraying insecticidal soap or neem oil will help control their numbers.'

organic_treatment_beginner.new: Wash them off with the hose, and pinch off any sprig that stays covered in them. Use insecticidal soap only if there are a lot.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: Removed 'More air and less stress usually fixes it', the beginner form of the same unanchored airflow-and-stress claim.
organic_treatment_beginner.anchor: clemson_hgic (herb-general scope): 'good sanitation, removal of weak or infested growth, and regular pruning' | uf_ifas (Pasco, TEMPLATE-WEAK): 'Use a strong jet of water to dislodge aphids from the plant.'

prevention_seasoned.new: Full sun, lean soil, room between plants, and restraint with the watering can. Lean ground helps because it does not push the soft, succulent growth aphids multiply on, not because a fast-growing plant fights them off; heavy feeding buys weak, sprawling stems and less flavor along with the aphids.
prevention_seasoned.why: THE HEADLINE FIX. The record said this practice keeps thyme 'vigorous enough to shrug off aphids', which states the mechanism backwards: aphids favor rapid succulent growth, so lean soil works by not producing it. As written the record taught a reader that pushing a plant harder is aphid protection, which inverts the advice on every crop they would generalize it to. The practice is right and is kept; the reason is replaced.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: clemson_hgic (herb-general scope): 'Aphids are common in rapidly growing, succulent plants that are in crowded conditions.' | iastate_ext: 'Apply fertilizer sparingly, if at all. Excess fertility can produce weak, sprawling growth and diminish the concentration of aromatic oils.'

prevention_beginner.new: Grow thyme in full sun with space around each plant, in poor dry soil, and go easy on fertilizer and water. Aphids go for soft, sappy growth, and lean soil is what keeps thyme from making any.
prevention_beginner.why: 'Healthy plants rarely get aphids' is the beginner form of the same inverted mechanism and is the sentence a beginner is most likely to act on, so it is corrected rather than softened.
prevention_beginner.anchor: clemson_hgic (herb-general scope): 'Aphids are common in rapidly growing, succulent plants that are in crowded conditions.' | iastate_ext: 'Apply fertilizer sparingly, if at all. Excess fertility can produce weak, sprawling growth.'

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is a wet-soil disease with no spray behind it. What decides the outcome is where you put the plant: a slope, a raised bed, gravelly ground, or a pot with plenty of drainage holes, and never the low corner that stays damp after rain.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Drainage is the whole control: nothing available to a home gardener saves a crown that is already rotting. Thyme will take poor, rocky ground that would starve most plants, so moving it or building the bed up beats trying to improve a heavy wet spot in place.

control_ladder.note_beginner: In a hot, humid region, pick one of the taller, smooth-leaved culinary thymes instead of a low, woolly creeping type: they cope with heat and damp air better. That is the plant coping with the climate, not beating the rot, so it belongs on top of good drainage and never in place of it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Thyme is a Mediterranean plant, and in humid regions the taller smooth-leaved species tolerate the heat and damp where the low woolly types struggle. This is tolerance of the conditions that bring the rot on rather than resistance to the organisms themselves, so it shifts the odds without settling them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A plant whose roots and base have rotted will not recover, so lift it out and dispose of it rather than waiting to see. Clear the dead material away instead of leaving it lying under the neighbors.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Take the loss out promptly and put the effort back into the site: overwatering and pooling do damage to an herb that is not reversible, so a collapsed plant is not something a change of watering habit rescues.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Yellowing, wilting and dieback on a plant that only worsens the more it is watered. Wet, poorly drained ground is behind it, and it is the single biggest killer of thyme.
symptoms_seasoned.why: Two fixes. (1) 'rather than to cold' is refuted: UMD couples the two rather than opposing them, and ISU reports winter injury as a separate real loss mode, so the record turned 'the usual cause is wet soil' (true) into 'cold is not a cause' (false). (2) 'often with a darkened, decayed base at the soil line' is anchorable only through UMD's southern blight page, which this entry does not admit (see notes_to_orchestrator), so it is dropped rather than left standing unsourced.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: iastate_ext: 'Most problems result from excessive moisture and poor drainage. Root rots and other fungal diseases may develop in wet soils.' + 'Overwatering can lead to root rot and reduced vigor.' | umd_ext: 'Poorly drained soil, water that pools due to the slope or plants being overwatered can cause irreversible damage to herbs.'

symptoms_beginner.new: The leaves yellow and the plant collapses while the soil around it is still wet. This is what kills most thyme plants, and it comes from ground that stays too damp.
symptoms_beginner.why: Drops 'often with a dark, rotted spot at the base' for the same reason as the seasoned register: the soil-line lesion is described only on UMD's southern blight page, which this entry does not admit.
symptoms_beginner.anchor: iastate_ext: 'Overwatering can lead to root rot and reduced vigor.' + 'Wet or poorly drained locations should be avoided because thyme is susceptible to root diseases in saturated soils.'

cause_seasoned.new: Soilborne rots that get going in saturated, badly drained ground and destroy the roots and crown from below. Thyme is intolerant of wet feet and waterlogged soil is the usual cause, but cold is not ruled out: wet, cold soil over winter is a documented way Mediterranean herbs like thyme are lost, and winter injury on the woody stems is a separate risk after a hard winter.
cause_seasoned.why: 'Waterlogged ground, not cold, is the underlying cause' is an authoring addition that inverts a real mechanism. UMD couples wet and cold in one sentence about thyme by name, and ISU reports winter injury separately. The same construction appears on oregano's root rot from a different agent, so it is a template twin carrying a wrong claim across crops; these sentences are written from the documents rather than from the sibling.
cause_seasoned.anchor: umd_ext: 'Excessively wet, cold soil can cause Mediterranean herbs such as rosemary, thyme, and lavenders to die over the winter.' | iastate_ext: 'Winter injury can also occur on woody stems, particularly after severe winters.' | ncsu_ext: 'They are intolerant to wet soils or poor drainage.'

cause_beginner.new: A rot in the soil that gets going where the ground stays soggy and drains slowly, killing the roots and the crown at soil level. Wet soil is the usual cause, and soil that is both wet and cold over winter can kill thyme in cold regions.
cause_beginner.why: 'The real cause is wet soil, not cold weather' is the beginner form of the refuted claim and is the flatter, more quotable version of it. Correcting the seasoned register alone would leave the wrong statement live in the register more readers see.
cause_beginner.anchor: umd_ext: 'Excessively wet, cold soil can cause Mediterranean herbs such as rosemary, thyme, and lavenders to die over the winter.' | iastate_ext: 'Winter injury can also occur on woody stems, particularly after severe winters.'

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: Once the roots and crown are rotting the damage is not reversible, so lift affected plants out and destroy them; nursing one along does not work. Everything worth doing on this one is drainage, done before the fact.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: The record asserted 'There is no cure once the crown is rotting' flatly. I kept the claim but scoped it to the wording of the source that carries it. CORRECTED after review: my first rationale said 'no thyme document states it', which was an absence I had not verified. The uf_ifas Pasco thyme post does state it ('There is no saving a plant with root rot', relayed by the independent reviewer, not read by me). That does not change the prose or the anchor, since Pasco is the find-and-replace template and umd_ext's 'irreversible damage' is the better warrant, but the rationale overstated an absence and is corrected rather than left standing.
organic_treatment_seasoned.anchor: umd_ext (herb-general scope): 'Poorly drained soil, water that pools due to the slope or plants being overwatered can cause irreversible damage to herbs.' | iastate_ext: 'Good drainage, proper spacing, and periodic replacement of aging plants help minimize these issues.'

organic_treatment_beginner.new: Once the roots and the base have gone soft there is no bringing the plant back, so dig it out and throw it away. What helps is drainage from the start, not a cure later on.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: Same scoping fix as the seasoned register: 'there is no fix' becomes 'will not recover', which is what the herb-general source's 'irreversible damage' supports.
organic_treatment_beginner.anchor: umd_ext (herb-general scope): 'can cause irreversible damage to herbs' | iastate_ext: 'Wet or poorly drained locations should be avoided because thyme is susceptible to root diseases in saturated soils.'

prevention_seasoned.new: Site it in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun, err on the dry side with water, and keep thyme out of ground that holds moisture. On heavy soil grow it raised or in a container of fast-draining mix, space plants so the ground dries between waterings, and in hot, humid regions favor the taller, smooth-leaved culinary types over the low woolly ones.
prevention_seasoned.why: Two changes. (1) The variety guidance is rescued here from the retired 'Foliar fungal problems in humid weather' entry: it is thyme-scoped, sourced and useful, and the humid-region risk it addresses is the one this entry manages. (2) 'use a mound or raised bed' kept but repointed: its only thyme-document sentence sat in the retired entry's powdery mildew paragraph, so the raised-bed half now rides on the improve_drainage method's own anchor while the container half takes a thyme-scoped source.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: clemson_hgic (thyme-scoped): 'In general, the taller growing species and those with smooth leaves will tolerate heat and humidity better than low growing or wooly types.' + 'Plant thyme in full sun in very well drained soil that stays dry.' | csu_ext: 'Thyme grows well in containers, especially indoors. Do not overwater due to root rot susceptibility.' | iastate_ext: 'Good drainage, proper spacing, and periodic replacement of aging plants help minimize these issues.' | RAISED BED HALF: carried by the improve_drainage method entry (its own anchor ucanr_ext, https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn74133.html), not by a thyme document. Flagged in notes_to_orchestrator.

prevention_beginner.new: Give it fast-draining soil and full sun, water on the light side, and keep it out of ground that stays soggy. Where the soil is heavy clay, grow it raised or in a pot, and in humid areas pick one of the taller, leafier kinds rather than a low fuzzy one.
prevention_beginner.why: Same two changes as the seasoned register, in plain words: the rescued variety guidance arrives, and the raised-bed advice is retained on the method's warrant rather than on the cross-applied powdery mildew sentence.
prevention_beginner.anchor: clemson_hgic (thyme-scoped): 'the taller growing species and those with smooth leaves will tolerate heat and humidity better than low growing or wooly types' | csu_ext: 'Thyme grows well in containers, especially indoors. Do not overwater due to root rot susceptibility.' | ncsu_ext: 'They prefer well-drained soils and can tolerate drought once they are established. They are intolerant to wet soils or poor drainage.'

unreachable_claims: RENEWAL OF AN AGEING CLUMP. iastate_ext puts 'periodic replacement of aging plants' in the same sentence as drainage and spacing as a way to minimize thyme's root and fungal problems, and ucanr_marin_mg says 'It will become woody with age and the center starts to die out after a few years. Replace it or propagate cuttings from the old plant.' NO method in the 64 carries replacing or renewing a declining woody perennial. certified_clean_stock is about the material you buy or propagate from, not about retiring a plant you already have, and crop_rotation is an annual-bed method. Filed, not forced: I did not bend either one to carry it. It is a real, twice-sourced cultural control for thyme's highest-severity problem and the only rung the ladder is genuinely missing.

REGULAR PRUNING AS A PEST MEASURE. clemson_hgic's herb-general sentence is 'The best defenses against pests on herbs are proper growing conditions, good sanitation, removal of weak or infested growth, and regular pruning.' The sanitation and removal halves are carried by garden_sanitation, but there is no method for routine pruning against an INSECT or MITE problem: prune_out_infection is physical and scoped bacterial / disease_general, so it cannot reach either of thyme's pest entries. This is the same two-class shape as the even_watering gap already filed in the brief.

NOT UNREACHABLE, DELIBERATELY NOT USED: sulfur. The pinned type flip from insect to mite makes sulfur legal for spider mites under control_ladder_gate. No document read recommends sulfur, or any chemical, on thyme for anything, and the horticultural_oil method entry warns against sulfur within two weeks of an oil spray. Recording it so the next pass does not read its absence as an oversight.
refusals: I did not author any powdery mildew, leaf spot or gray mold claim anywhere in thyme's record, including as a surviving sentence relocated out of the retired entry. No admitted source names a foliar fungal pathogen on Thymus; the one document that names powdery mildew published the identical paragraph about oregano with the crop name swapped.

I did not write an aromatic-oil deterrence rationale for thyme's low pest load, even though the sibling precedent exists on lemongrass. No document read attributes thyme's low pest load to its essential oils, and iastate_ext's only oil statement runs the other way: over-fertilizing 'diminish[es] the concentration of aromatic oils'.

I did not author a biological rung on either pest entry. Nothing read publishes a natural-enemy statement for aphids or mites on thyme, so a beneficial_predators or augmentative_release rung would have been written off a generic document with no crop warrant. Three and four rungs is what the evidence pays for.

I did not author a soft_chemical or conventional rung on root and crown rot. Nothing read recommends a fungicide for thyme root rot, so the ladder is cultural-only. That is unusual enough to state rather than pad around, and it is why that entry has three rungs to the mite entry's three and the aphid entry's four.

I did not pin a binomial anywhere. No thyme-scoped document read names a mite species, an aphid species, or an admitted-catalog pathogen for the rot. The entries stay at common-name level, which is what the sources support.

I did not write a threshold, a count, or a treat-at trigger on either pest entry. No document read publishes one for thyme, and the ladder must not invent the number that would make it feel more precise.

I did not build prose on the UF/IFAS Pasco 'Spice Up Your Life' post's wording, per the dispatch instruction, and I have not treated it as independent corroboration of anything. It is cited on the two pest entries because it is the only thyme-titled document that names those pests and their treatments, and every field_correction that leans on it is marked TEMPLATE-WEAK in its anchor string.
notes_to_orchestrator: THE RETIRED ENTRY, ANSWERED DIRECTLY: yes, exactly ONE sentence from 'Foliar fungal problems in humid weather' deserves to survive, and I have moved it. clemson_hgic's thyme-scoped variety guidance ('In general, the taller growing species and those with smooth leaves will tolerate heat and humidity better than low growing or wooly types') is now (a) the resistant_varieties rung on crown-and-root-rot and (b) a declared correction to that entry's prevention_seasoned and prevention_beginner. It goes there rather than to crop-level prose because the humid-region risk it addresses is the risk this entry manages, and because as a ladder rung it is actionable at the moment a reader is choosing a plant. If you would rather it also appear in the crop's descriptive prose, that is a crop-level field outside my declared set and I have not touched it.

WHAT FROM THE RETIRED ENTRY DOES NOT SURVIVE, AND WHY. (1) The symptom list 'powdery white film, spots, or grayish mold' is three diseases in one clause and no admitted source reports any of them on thyme; it is dropped, not relocated. (2) 'Water at the base rather than overhead' and 'open up airflow' read as rescuable but are not: their warrant is csu_ext's herb-general splashing sentence and umn_ext's crowding sentence, both FOLIAR-disease rationales. Moving them onto a root-zone entry would be reading a leaf-disease document into a root-disease claim, which is the reviewer's own point 4. Spacing survives on the rot entry only in the form iastate_ext itself anchors to root disease ('Good drainage, proper spacing, and periodic replacement of aging plants help minimize these issues'), phrased as letting the ground dry rather than as canopy airflow. (3) The post-bloom shear is real thyme husbandry (iastate_ext, csu_ext) but is not a disease control in any document; it belongs in crop-level care prose and no method carries it.
